title: Chapter 4.  History — Dogra Conquest to the 2019 Reorganisation

blocks.content: This chapter bridges Ladakh's independent-kingdom history (Chapter 3) to its present-day UT status, tracing its absorption into the Dogra princely state, its place within the erstwhile State of Jammu and Kashmir, and its eventual separation as its own Union Territory in 2019.

General Zorawar Singh, a military commander serving under the Dogra ruler Gulab Singh of Jammu, led a series of military campaigns that conquered Ladakh in 1834, ending the independent Namgyal kingdom and incorporating the region into Dogra-controlled territory.

Zorawar Singh subsequently led further campaigns extending Dogra control into Baltistan (1840) and, most ambitiously, into western Tibet (1841), though this Tibet campaign ultimately failed disastrously - Zorawar Singh himself was killed in battle at Taklakot in December 1841, and the resulting conflict was concluded by the Treaty of Chushul (1842), which restored the pre-war Ladakh-Tibet boundary while confirming Dogra sovereignty over Ladakh itself.

Following the 1846 Treaty of Amritsar's creation of the wider Dogra princely state of Jammu and Kashmir (detailed in the companion J&K GS volume), Ladakh was administratively absorbed into this larger state as one of its constituent regions, a status it retained through the rest of the Dogra period and into independent India.

★ EXAM POINT: General Zorawar Singh's Ladakh conquest (1834) predates the 1846 Treaty of Amritsar (which formally created the Dogra princely state) by 12 years - Ladakh was conquered under Gulab Singh's own initiative as a Jammu-based Dogra chieftain BEFORE he became the formally recognised Maharaja of the new princely state.
Ladakh Within the Erstwhile State of Jammu and Kashmir (1947-2019)

items: Following Maharaja Hari Singh's 1947 Instrument of Accession to India, Ladakh became part of independent India as a region of the state of Jammu and Kashmir, subject to the same Article 370 special-status framework that applied to the state as a whole.

Ladakh's own political history within the erstwhile state included periodic local movements for greater autonomy or separate status, reflecting long-standing concerns (particularly from the Buddhist-majority Leh area) about political and developmental marginalisation within a state whose politics were often dominated by the more populous Kashmir Valley.

The Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (LAHDCs) for Leh and Kargil were established under separate legislation in 1995 (Leh) and 2003 (Kargil) respectively, granting a significant degree of local self-governance over specified subjects even while Ladakh remained formally part of the wider state - an important institutional precursor to the region's post-2019 governance structure (Chapter 6).

blocks.content: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, effective from 31 October 2019, bifurcated the erstwhile state into two separate Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir (with a Legislative Assembly) and Ladakh (without a Legislative Assembly, comprising the Leh and Kargil districts).

This separation was, notably, WELCOMED relatively more warmly in parts of Ladakh (particularly the Buddhist-majority Leh area, whose political leadership had long sought separation from the Kashmir-Valley-dominated state government) than in the Kashmir Valley itself, though this initial welcome has since been substantially complicated by the region's subsequent, largely unmet demands for statehood and Sixth Schedule protection (Chapter 7) - meaning candidates should understand Ladakh's relationship with its 2019 status as considerably more nuanced and evolved than a simple binary of support or opposition.
31 October 2019, the effective date of separation, coincided with Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's birth anniversary, the same symbolic date chosen for the wider J&K reorganisation.

★ EXAM POINT: A frequently tested nuance: Ladakh's LEH-based leadership initially WELCOMED separation from J&K in 2019 (unlike much of the Kashmir Valley's political reaction) - but this initial welcome has since evolved into strong, sustained demands for STATEHOOD and Sixth Schedule protection (Chapter 7), since UT-without-Assembly status has proven administratively frustrating in practice.

items: General Zorawar Singh conquered Ladakh for the Dogras in 1834 (12 years before the 1846 Treaty of Amritsar formally created the J&K princely state).
Zorawar Singh's 1841 Tibet campaign failed; he was killed at Taklakot; Treaty of Chushul (1842) restored the Ladakh-Tibet boundary while confirming Dogra sovereignty over Ladakh.
LAHDCs (Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils) for Leh (1995) and Kargil (2003) pre-date the 2019 UT status.
31 October 2019: J&K Reorganisation Act takes effect - Ladakh becomes a separate UT (Leh + Kargil districts), without a Legislative Assembly.
Leh's leadership initially welcomed 2019 separation from J&K; this has since evolved into strong demands for statehood/Sixth Schedule protection (Chapter 7).
